question_text:
The MCU below can only source 5 mA per GPIO pin, but the LED needs 20 mA to reach its rated brightness. The Vcc rail can supply ample current.

How do you drive the LED at 20 mA without exceeding the GPIO pin limit?
answer_text:
Use a low-side N-channel MOSFET (NFET) switch. The GPIO drives the gate; the Vcc rail supplies the LED current through the resistor and transistor.

▶ Detailed Explanation

The NFET gate draws essentially zero DC current (gate is insulated from channel). The GPIO only has to charge the gate capacitance — a tiny burst, well under 5 mA.

The LED current path is entirely separate: Vcc → R → LED → NFET drain → source → GND. The transistor acts as a voltage-controlled switch.

Resistor value: V_R = 3.3V − 2V = 1.3V. At 20 mA: R = 1.3V / 20 mA = 65 Ω → standard value 68 Ω (gives ≈ 19 mA).

GPIO HIGH → NFET ON → LED ON. GPIO LOW → NFET OFF → LED OFF.

This is called a low-side switch because the transistor sits between the load and GND (the low side of the supply).
bonus_question_text: What do you look for when picking the NFET for this circuit?
bonus_answer_text:
Four things to check on the datasheet:

1. Gate threshold voltage (Vth)

The NFET must turn on fully with your GPIO voltage. Use a logic-level MOSFET with Vth ≤ 1.5V so a 3.3V GPIO drives it into full saturation. Standard MOSFETs often need 5–10V on the gate.

2. Continuous drain current (Id)

Must exceed your LED current with margin. For 20 mA, any MOSFET rated ≥ 100 mA is fine — logic-level devices like the 2N7002 (200 mA) are typical choices.

3. Power dissipation

In saturation the MOSFET's on-resistance (Rds_on) is tiny (e.g. 5 Ω). Power = I² × Rds_on = (20 mA)² × 5 Ω = 2 mW — negligible. Only matters at higher currents.

4. High-side vs low-side

This circuit is low-side (NFET between load and GND) — the simplest topology for N-channel FETs since source is at GND, making gate drive straightforward. A high-side N-channel switch needs the gate driven above Vcc, which requires a bootstrap or charge-pump circuit.

PWM note

PWM works exactly the same as with a direct GPIO drive — toggle the gate signal at your target frequency. The NFET switches fast enough (nanoseconds) that it tracks PWM signals up to hundreds of kHz without issue.
